course.title: Java Beginner Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive beginner course for the Java programming language. Covers variables, data types, OOP, collections, exception handling, file I/O, generics, lambdas, streams, and a capstone project. Designed for complete beginners with detailed explanations that gradually become more concise.

blocks.value: What is Java?

Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1995 and is now owned by Oracle. Java's motto is 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA) — compiled Java code runs on any platform that has a Java Virtual Machine (JVM).
Where is Java Used?

Java powers a massive portion of the software world:
• Enterprise Applications: Banking systems, insurance platforms, ERP systems (Spring, Jakarta EE)
• Android Development: Native Android apps are built with Java (and Kotlin)
• Web Backend: Spring Boot is the most popular Java framework for REST APIs
• Big Data: Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark, Kafka are Java-based
• Cloud Services: Netflix, Amazon, LinkedIn use Java for microservices
• Desktop Applications: IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, Minecraft
• Embedded Systems: Smart cards, IoT devices, set-top boxes
How Java Differs from Other Languages

Java vs Python: Java is statically typed and compiled, Python is dynamically typed and interpreted. Java is faster for large applications; Python is faster to write small scripts.

Java vs C++: Java has automatic memory management (garbage collection), C++ requires manual memory management. Java runs on a VM; C++ compiles to native machine code.

Java vs JavaScript: Completely different languages despite similar names. Java is compiled and strongly typed; JavaScript is interpreted and dynamically typed.

Java vs Rust: Java has a garbage collector and simpler memory model; Rust uses ownership for memory safety without GC. Java has a larger ecosystem; Rust has better performance for systems programming.
Why Top Companies Choose Java

Companies like Google, Amazon, Netflix, Uber, Spotify, and banks worldwide use Java because:
• Mature Ecosystem: 30+ years of libraries, frameworks, and tooling
• Strong Typing: Catches errors at compile time, reducing runtime bugs
• JVM Performance: JIT compilation makes Java surprisingly fast
• Massive Talent Pool: Easy to hire Java developers globally
• Enterprise-Grade: Built-in security, concurrency, and monitoring
• Backward Compatibility: Code written in Java 1.0 still runs today
• Spring Ecosystem: Spring Boot makes building microservices incredibly productive

blocks.value: Every Java program needs at least one class. The class name must match the filename (HelloWorld.java → public class HelloWorld). The main method is the entry point — it's where execution begins. public static void main(String[] args) is the exact signature the JVM looks for.
Compiling and Running

# Compile (creates HelloWorld.class bytecode file)
javac HelloWorld.java

# Run (JVM executes the bytecode)
java HelloWorld

blocks.question: What does WORA stand for in Java?
blocks.explanation: WORA means compiled Java bytecode runs on any platform with a JVM, without recompilation.

blocks.question: What is the entry point method signature in Java?
blocks.explanation: The JVM looks for exactly this signature: public static void main(String[] args). Any deviation and the program won't run.

blocks.question: What command compiles a .java file into bytecode?
blocks.explanation: javac (Java Compiler) compiles .java source files into .class bytecode files that the JVM can execute.

blocks.value: Storing Data in Java

Java is a statically typed language — every variable must have a declared type, and that type cannot change. This catches errors early at compile time. Java has two categories of data types: primitives (stored directly) and reference types (stored as references to objects).

blocks.question: Which integer type is the default in Java?
blocks.explanation: When you write a whole number literal like 42, Java treats it as int by default. Use L suffix for long.

blocks.question: What keyword makes a variable constant (cannot be reassigned)?
blocks.explanation: final makes a variable immutable after initialization. For primitives, the value can't change. For objects, the reference can't change (but object state can).

blocks.question: What suffix is required for a float literal like 3.14?
blocks.explanation: Floating literals like 3.14 are double by default. Append f or F to make them float: 3.14f.

blocks.question: What is the result of 17 / 5 in Java?
blocks.explanation: When both operands are integers, / performs integer division and truncates the decimal. 17 / 5 = 3, not 3.4.

blocks.question: What is short-circuit evaluation?
options: Skipping the second operand if the result is already determined
blocks.correctAnswer: Skipping the second operand if the result is already determined
blocks.explanation: In (false && anything), the second operand isn't evaluated because the result is already false. This prevents errors like division by zero.

blocks.question: What operator assigns a value based on a condition?
blocks.explanation: The ternary operator ? : is a shorthand for if-else: condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false.

blocks.value: Loops

blocks.question: What happens if you forget break in a switch case?
blocks.explanation: Without break, execution 'falls through' to the next case. This is sometimes intentional but often a bug. Use the arrow syntax (Java 14+) to avoid this.

blocks.question: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
blocks.explanation: do-while checks the condition AFTER executing the body, so it always runs at least once. while and for check before.

blocks.question: What keyword skips the current iteration and continues to the next?
blocks.explanation: continue skips the rest of the current loop iteration and proceeds to the next one. break exits the loop entirely.

blocks.value: Strings are immutable in Java — every 'modification' creates a new String object. For frequent modifications, use StringBuilder (not thread-safe) or StringBuffer (thread-safe). Use == for reference comparison; use .equals() for content comparison.

blocks.question: How do you compare two Strings for equal content?
blocks.explanation: == compares references (memory addresses). .equals() compares the actual character content. Always use .equals() for String comparison.

blocks.question: Which class should you use for mutable strings in a single thread?
blocks.explanation: StringBuilder is faster than StringBuffer because it's not synchronized (not thread-safe). Use StringBuffer only when multiple threads modify the same string.

blocks.question: What property gives the number of elements in an array?
blocks.explanation: Arrays have a length property (not a method): arr.length. Strings have a length() method: str.length().

blocks.value: Defining Reusable Code Blocks

Methods are reusable blocks of code that perform a specific task. They improve code organization, reduce duplication, and make programs easier to maintain. Every method has a signature (name + parameters) and a body.

blocks.value: Java is strictly pass-by-value. For primitives, the value is copied. For objects, the reference (memory address) is copied — so you can modify the object's contents but cannot reassign the original reference.

blocks.question: What is required for method overloading?
blocks.explanation: Overloading requires different parameter types, counts, or order. Return type alone is not sufficient for overloading.

blocks.question: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
blocks.explanation: Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the reference value is copied. You can modify object contents but cannot change the caller's reference variable.

blocks.question: What keyword indicates a method returns no value?
blocks.explanation: void indicates the method returns nothing. Methods with a return type must use the return keyword to send back a value.

blocks.value: Object-Oriented Programming in Java

Java is fundamentally object-oriented. A class is a blueprint for creating objects. An object is an instance of a class. Classes encapsulate data (fields/attributes) and behavior (methods) into a single unit.

blocks.question: What keyword creates a new object instance?
blocks.explanation: The new keyword allocates memory and calls the constructor to create a new object instance: new ClassName().

blocks.question: What does the this keyword refer to?
blocks.explanation: this refers to the current object instance. It's used to disambiguate fields from parameters and for method chaining.

blocks.question: What is a special method that initializes a new object called?
blocks.explanation: A constructor has the same name as the class and no return type. It runs automatically when an object is created with new.

blocks.question: Which access modifier makes a member accessible only within its own class?
blocks.explanation: private is the most restrictive. The member is only accessible within the class it's declared in.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of getters and setters?
options: To control access and validate data
blocks.correctAnswer: To control access and validate data

blocks.question: What keyword makes a variable belong to the class rather than instances?
blocks.explanation: static members belong to the class, not individual objects. There's only one copy shared across all instances.

blocks.question: What keyword establishes inheritance in Java?
blocks.explanation: class Child extends Parent establishes an inheritance relationship. implements is used for interfaces.

blocks.question: What annotation indicates a method overrides a parent method?
blocks.explanation: @Override tells the compiler to verify that the method actually overrides a parent method. It catches typos in method signatures.

blocks.question: What is the root class that every Java class implicitly extends?
blocks.explanation: Every class in Java implicitly extends java.lang.Object if no parent is specified. Object provides toString(), equals(), hashCode(), and other fundamental methods.

blocks.value: Polymorphism: Many Forms

Polymorphism means 'many forms.' In Java, it allows objects of different classes to be treated as objects of a common parent class. The same method call can behave differently based on the actual object's class. Combined with abstraction, it enables flexible, extensible designs.

blocks.value: Interfaces define contracts that classes must fulfill. A class can implement multiple interfaces (unlike inheritance which is single). Java 8+ added default and static methods to interfaces, allowing some implementation.

blocks.question: Can an abstract class be instantiated?
options: Yes, if it has no abstract methods
blocks.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated directly. They exist to be extended by concrete subclasses that implement all abstract methods.

blocks.question: How many interfaces can a class implement?
blocks.explanation: A class can implement multiple interfaces, separated by commas: class X implements A, B, C. This is Java's way of achieving multiple inheritance of type.

blocks.question: What keyword is used to implement an interface?
blocks.explanation: class MyClass implements MyInterface { ... }. extends is for classes; implements is for interfaces. A class can do both: extends Parent implements Interface1, Interface2.

blocks.value: Handling Errors Gracefully

Exceptions are events that disrupt the normal flow of program execution. Java uses a structured exception handling mechanism with try, catch, finally, throw, and throws. Exceptions are objects that extend the Throwable class hierarchy.
The Exception Hierarchy

Throwable is the root class. It has two direct subclasses:
• Error: Serious problems you shouldn't catch (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
• Exception: Conditions your program should catch
  - RuntimeException (unchecked): NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
  - Other exceptions (checked): IOException, SQLException

blocks.question: What block ALWAYS executes, whether an exception occurs or not?
blocks.explanation: The finally block executes under all circumstances — success, exception, or even return statements. It's used for cleanup like closing resources.

blocks.question: Which exceptions must be declared or handled?
blocks.explanation: Checked exceptions (non-RuntimeException subclasses of Exception) must be either caught or declared with throws. RuntimeException and Error are unchecked.

blocks.question: What keyword is used to declare that a method may throw an exception?
blocks.explanation: throws in the method signature declares checked exceptions that might be thrown. throw is used to actually throw an exception object.

blocks.value: When to Use Which

| Operation | ArrayList | LinkedList |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| Random access (get) | O(1) — Fast | O(n) — Slow |
| Add/remove at end | O(1) amortized | O(1) |
| Add/remove at middle | O(n) | O(n) (but faster in practice for small lists) |
| Add/remove at beginning | O(n) | O(1) |
| Memory overhead | Low | High (pointers) |

Use ArrayList for most cases. Use LinkedList only when you frequently add/remove at the beginning or need queue/stack behavior.

blocks.question: Which List implementation provides O(1) random access?
blocks.explanation: ArrayList uses a backing array, so get(index) is O(1). LinkedList must traverse from the head, making it O(n).

blocks.question: Does List allow duplicate elements?
blocks.explanation: List implementations (ArrayList, LinkedList) allow duplicate elements and maintain insertion order. Use Set if you need uniqueness.

blocks.question: What diamond operator syntax creates a typed ArrayList in Java 7+?
blocks.explanation: The diamond operator <> allows type inference: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); The compiler infers the type from the left side.

blocks.value: equals() and hashCode() Contract

blocks.output: Set size: 1

blocks.value: If two objects are equal (equals returns true), they MUST have the same hashCode. If hashCode differs, HashSet/HashMap will treat them as different even if equals says they're the same. Always override both together.

blocks.question: Which collection does NOT allow duplicate elements?
blocks.explanation: Set implementations (HashSet, TreeSet) reject duplicate elements. List allows duplicates. Map allows duplicate values but not duplicate keys.

blocks.question: What happens if equals() returns true but hashCode() differs?
options: HashSet/HashMap may treat them as different
blocks.correctAnswer: HashSet/HashMap may treat them as different
blocks.explanation: The hashCode contract requires equal objects to have equal hash codes. Violating this breaks hash-based collections.

blocks.question: What Map method returns a default value if the key is not found?
blocks.explanation: map.getOrDefault(key, defaultValue) returns the value for the key, or the default if the key doesn't exist. No null checking needed.

Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces, and methods. They provide compile-time type safety and eliminate the need for explicit casting.

blocks.value: PECS principle: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Use <? extends T> when reading (producing) values. Use <? super T> when writing (consuming) values.

blocks.question: What is the benefit of generics?
blocks.explanation: Generics catch type errors at compile time and eliminate manual casting. They use type erasure, so there's no runtime overhead.

blocks.question: What does <? extends Number> mean?
blocks.explanation: ? extends Number is an upper bounded wildcard. It accepts Number or any of its subclasses (Integer, Double, etc.).

blocks.question: What is the PECS principle mnemonic?
blocks.explanation: PECS: Use extends when reading (producing) from a collection, super when writing (consuming) to a collection.

blocks.question: Can enums have fields and methods?
blocks.explanation: Java enums are classes. They can have fields, constructors, methods, and even implement interfaces. Each constant is an instance.

blocks.question: What does @FunctionalInterface do?
options: Ensures the interface has exactly one abstract method
blocks.correctAnswer: Ensures the interface has exactly one abstract method
blocks.explanation: @FunctionalInterface is a compiler check. It ensures the interface is a valid functional interface (single abstract method) and can be used with lambdas.

blocks.question: What annotation marks a method that overrides a parent method?
blocks.explanation: @Override tells the compiler to verify the method actually overrides a parent method. It catches signature mismatches at compile time.
